sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
This paper presents miniaturized energy harvesters, where the frequency up-conversion technique is used to improve the bandwidth of vibration energy harvesters. The proposed and developed miniature piezoelectric energy harvester utilizes magnetic repulsion forces to achieve non-contact frequency up-conversion, thereby avoiding mechanical collision and wear for long-term working durability. A pair of piezoelectric resonant cantilevers is micro-fabricated to generate electric power. A simplified model involving linear oscillators and magnetic interaction is deployed to demonstrate the feasibility of the device design. A bench-top harvester has been fabricated and characterized, resulting in average power generation of over $1 0 \mu \mathrm { W }$ within a broad frequency range of $1 0 { - } 2 2 \mathrm { H z }$ under $_ { 1 g }$ acceleration.

(Some figures may appear in colour only in the online journal)

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Vibratory energy harvesting has aroused increasing research interest due to its potential application as a pervasive energy source [1–5]. Vibratory energy harvesters sense ambient vibrations and transform the mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic [6, 7], piezoelectric [8, 9] or electrostatic [10, 11] mechanisms. Although the power converted from ambient vibrations is usually small compared to other power sources such as solar cells, lithium ion batteries and micro fuel cells [3], it is adequate for properly designed autonomous systems with efficient power budgeting and low-power consumption electronic devices. Elfrink et al demonstrated an autonomous wireless sensor node fully powered by a piezoelectric MEMS energy harvester [12]. Besides, what the harvesters provide is really green energy. Commercialized energy harvesters have been increasingly available of late and have shown great potential in microsystem applications [13].

Vibratory energy harvesters are often implemented with linear oscillators that resonate at their natural frequencies, thereby maximizing power output. However, resonant harvesters exhibit narrow bandwidth despite their high peak power. Meanwhile, in many applications, the ambient vibration is not necessarily simple-harmonic or even nonperiodic, which greatly reduces energy harvesting efficiency. Moreover, when the ambient vibration frequency is very low, i.e. a few tens of hertz, the size of the resonant energy harvesters needs to be quite large to match the low frequency. With the size limited by the application system dimensions, a practical solution is to raise the oscillating frequency of the transducer parts [14].

To address this problem, structures other than linear resonators have been increasingly studied. Tunable harvesters can adapt to different frequencies by means of changing the effective stiffness of mechanical springs. Nevertheless, passive tuning often requires manual operation [15, 16] while active tuning lowers energy harvesting efficiency [17]. Using multiple (or arrayed) harvesters to cover a wide band of frequencies improves adaptability, yet it reduces power density [18]. The frequency up-conversion technique is a promising solution for non-periodic and/or low-frequency ambient vibrations. This type of harvester deploys nonlinearity to excite an oscillator at its natural frequency which is prominently higher than the ambient vibration frequency. Quite a lot of research has shown the feasibility and adaptability of such harvesters. Rastegar et al [19] proposed a mechanism, with a low-frequency oscillator plucking a secondary high-frequency transducer beam. Lee et al [20] designed and fabricated a similar plucking frequency upconversion energy harvester by using MEMS technology. Galchev et al [9] achieved frequency up-conversion using magnetic attraction. Unfortunately, all the above-mentioned designs involve physical wear and collision that no doubt reduces the durability of the devices. To solve this problem, non-contact magnetic driving methods have been proposed [21–25].

![](images/6f0bc5e3459221b4c82b18f08806b7989c6ff8ec932205c818a07ad4533ad5ad.jpg)  
Figure 1. 3D schematic (left) and structural layout (right) of the frequency up-conversion piezoelectric energy harvester.

This work presents a novel bi-stable frequency upconversion piezoelectric energy harvester that utilizes magnetic repulsive force to drive a frequency-increased generator (FIG). The harvester consists of a central sliding mass and a pair of FIGs that are composed of piezoelectric microcantilevers. Permanent magnets are mounted on both the central mass and the ends of the FIG cantilevers. Excited by ambient vibration, the sliding mass magnet moves back and forth and intermittently repels the FIG end magnets by mutually repulsive magnetic force. The FIG cantilevers are forced to bend and then released after the sliding mass moves away. In this way, the FIGs freely vibrate at their identical natural frequency, which is much higher than that of the ambient vibration. The frequency up-conversion mechanism is modeled using simplified linear oscillators and dipole-based magnetic interaction. A miniature harvester has been designed, fabricated and experimentally characterized.

sections.heading: 2. Design and modeling
sections.text:
Figure 1 schematically shows the structure of the frequency upconversion harvester. The central sliding mass is constrained within an in-wall lubricated tube. Permanent magnets are fixed on the central mass and both ends of the tube, forming a nonlinear oscillator. FIGs are a pair of piezoelectric microcantilevers with an end magnet on each.

The mechanical structure of the energy harvester is modeled and shown in figure 2(a). The FIG is modeled as a linear mass–spring system, with the spring constant $k _ { \mathrm { F } }$ , the effective end mass $m _ { \mathrm { F } }$ and the damping coefficient $c _ { \mathrm { F } }$ extracted from the dimensions as well as the masses of the cantilever beam and the end magnet. The central mass $m _ { \mathrm { C } }$ is repelled by both the tube-end magnets and the FIG end magnets. Excited by external vibration, the central mass travels past the FIGs intermittently and repels their end magnets. The FIG cantilever beams bend until the restoring force is large enough to prevent further deflection and then start to freely vibrate till the next repulsion from the central magnet. This vibration frequency is about one order of magnitude higher than the external vibration frequency, thereby realizing the frequency up-conversion. The equations of motion (EOMs) governing the system are

$$
\ddot { z } _ { \mathrm { C } } = - a _ { \mathrm { e x t } } \sin ( \omega t + \theta ) + ( F _ { \mathrm { E - C } } + F _ { \mathrm { F - C } } ) / m _ { \mathrm { C } }
$$

$$
\ddot { z } _ { \mathrm { F } } = - a _ { \mathrm { e x t } } \sin ( \omega t + \theta ) - ( k _ { \mathrm { F } } z _ { \mathrm { F } } + F _ { \mathrm { F - C } } + c _ { \mathrm { F } } \dot { z } _ { \mathrm { F } } ) / m _ { \mathrm { F } } .
$$

As noted in figure 2(a), $z _ { \mathrm { C } }$ and $z _ { \mathrm { F } }$ are $z$ -axis displacements of the central mass and the FIG, respectively. $a _ { \mathrm { e x t } } \sin ( \omega t + \theta )$ is the input acceleration induced by the external vibration. $F _ { \mathrm { E - C } }$ is the $z$ component of the magnetic force between the central mass magnet and the tube-terminal magnets. $F _ { \mathrm { F - C } }$ is the $z$ component of the magnetic forces between the central mass magnet and the FIG magnets. Other components are neglected due to structure symmetry and the minor effect on FIG characteristics. A cuboidal magnet model is herein applied in the simulation for computational simplicity. Calculation of the magnetic forces is based on magnetic dipole interactions [26]. For the two cuboidal magnets that are both magnetized in the z direction, the $z$ component of the magnetic force between them can be expressed as

$$
\begin{array} { c } { { F _ { z } = \displaystyle \frac { J _ { 1 } J _ { 2 } } { 4 \pi \mu _ { 0 } } \sum \sum \sum \sum \sum \sum \sum } _ { ( i , j , k , l , p , q = \{ 0 , 1 \} ^ { 6 } ) } }  \\ { { \times ( - 1 ) ^ { i + j + k + l + p + q } \phi _ { z } ( i , j , k , l , p , q ) } } \end{array}

where $J _ { 1 }$ and $J _ { 2 }$ are the magnetizations of the two magnets. $\phi _ { z }$ is a function of the geometries of the magnets, with its expression given in equation (5) of [26]. For $F _ { \mathrm { E - C } }$ and $F _ { \mathrm { F - C } }$ substituting with the related geometrical parameters can yield the corresponding forces.

From equations (1) and (2) we obtain the time-domain displacements of the central mass and the FIG ends under sinusoidal external vibrations, as is shown in figure 3(a). The harvester parameters used in our design and simulation are listed in table 1. The FIG ends are repelled when the central mass approaches and are then released when the magnetic repulsive force no longer compresses the springs. The FIGs are then vibrating at their resonant frequency, realizing frequency up-conversion. When the input frequency is too high for the central mass to respond, the FIGs would not be effectively driven and the central mass would simply vibrate between one tube-end magnet and the FIGs with small amplitude, as is shown in figure 3(b).

sections.heading: 3. Fabrication
sections.text:
A miniature piezoelectric energy harvester has been fabricated, as is shown in figure 4. The central mass is made from a cylindrical NdFeB magnet and an additional tungsten mass. It is housed in a teflon tube whose inner wall is lubricated with graphite. Part of the tube is thinned so that the gaps between the central magnet and the FIG magnets can be sufficiently small. Tube-end magnets are fixed on bolted fixtures, making it easier to assemble the central mass and the tube. The FIG micro-cantilevers are fabricated by bonding a $3 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { { m } }$ thick polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) piezoelectric film on a $5 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ thick copper foil with cyanoacrylate adhesive. The piezoelectric film (provided by Jinzhou KeXin Electronic Materials Co. Ltd) is pre-coated with Al electrode layers on both sides for the electrical lead-out. The composite film is patterned into a $9 \mathrm { m m } \times 1 . 3 \mathrm { m m }$ cantilever shape and adhered with the end magnets. The cantilevers have their roots clampfixed. The harvester is finally assembled on a Bakelite board. The geometric dimensions and the tested magnetic strength of the magnets in the fabricated harvester is listed in table 2. Table 1. sections.heading: 4. Testing results and discussion
sections.text:
Testing is performed to characterize the fabricated device. The harvester is mounted on a Br¨uel & Kjær 4808 shaker that provides sinusoidal ambient vibration. Each FIG is loaded with a $6 . 1 \ \mathrm { M } \Omega$ matching resistor. The output voltage is measured along with the vibration frequency increases. The frequency sweeping starts from $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ due to accuracy limitations of the instruments, and ends as the output voltage drops to nearly zero. ![](images/c950ab9a39fd647db7ac70816fa033aec0bd762697ec9464a2a128cd99a75c9e.jpg) Figure 5. Figure 5 shows the operation of the energy harvester under an external sinusoidal acceleration of $_ { 1 g }$ at $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . It can be seen that the FIGs are repelled twice every 0.1 s and vibrate at $2 4 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , i.e. the resonant frequency. During the entire testing, the harvester generates a peak power of $1 0 1 . 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ and an average power of $1 4 . 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ at $_ { 1 g }$ and $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ . The waveforms from the two FIGs are not exactly symmetrical due to the fabrication tolerance such as the complex interaction between the magnets, loose constraints of the central mass and the FIG patterning precision. The device is also tested under accelerations of 2 and $_ { 3 g }$ , yielding higher powers. Figure 6 illustrates the average power output versus frequency at $1 g , 2 g$ and $_ { 3 g }$ , respectively. As input acceleration increases, the lower limit of the frequency sweeping also increases due to accuracy limitations. The bandwidth of the harvester is limited by the central mass and the tube-end magnets, which form a nonlinear oscillator. When the central mass fails to respond to the varying inertial force field, it simply vibrates between one tube-terminal magnet and the FIGs, thereby causing a small vibration amplitude and halting the frequency up-conversion procedure. As can be seen in figure 6, increase of the external acceleration improves bandwidth significantly but makes a limited contribution to power gain. A larger acceleration helps to compensate the accelerating process of the central mass with more kinetic energy so that the mass can drive the FIGs, thereby well sustaining our frequency up-conversion mechanism. However, given a certain frequency, an input acceleration which is too large easily causes the central mass to collide with the tube-terminal magnets, which in turn limits its kinetic energy and dissipates excess power. Further improvement can be made by adjusting the positions of the tube-end masses to adapt to different frequency bands. ![](images/fbf8b39af728e76f2d126cb3c4510e6e790a5d4090ebbdcd77b04cfc3ca1297a.jpg) Figure 7. Table 3 compares the tested performance of our harvester with published works that were designed for operation at low frequencies. For electric power-supply applications, the AC output from the harvester needs to be rectified and filtered to provide DC power. Under an acceleration of $_ { 1 g }$ at $1 0 \ \mathrm { H z }$ , we test the device interfaced with a simple rectifier and a storage capacitor (schematically shown in figure 7(a)). The full-bridge rectifier consists of four 1N-4148 diodes. Figure 7(b) illustrates the tested charging curve of the storage capacitor. The charging power is estimated of the order of $0 . 1 \mu \mathrm { W }$ . Though this output is far less than the output under matched load and needs to be further improved, the device may find application in low-power microsystems.

sections.heading: 5. Conclusion
sections.text: This paper presents the design, fabrication and test of a miniature frequency up-conversion piezoelectric energy harvester with power generating capability at low frequency over a wide frequency range. Frequency up-conversion is achieved by utilizing magnetic repulsion force that avoids mechanical collision and wear, thereby improving durability. With an input acceleration of $_ { 1 g }$ , the fabricated device generates a peak power of $1 0 1 . 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ and an average power of $1 4 . 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ at $1 0 ~ \mathrm { H z }$ , and generates more than $1 0 ~ \mu \mathrm { W }$ over the frequency range of $1 0 { - } 2 2 \ \mathrm { ~ H z }$ . An electromechanical model involving nonlinearity is currently being developed to better predict the behavior of such non-contact frequency upconversion harvesters. Variances of the harvester are being considered to improve performance by structural optimization and more compact frequency up-conversion configuration.
